headline: Massachusetts colleges may have to disclose closure risk by Dec. 31
dek: Higher-education officials are planning an earlier public-warning deadline for financially distressed private colleges after two Massachusetts schools announced plans to close last spring.
body: Massachusetts higher-education officials are planning to require private colleges and universities judged to be at risk of imminent closure to post a public notice by Dec. 31, an effort to give students, employees and surrounding communities more time to respond to a financial crisis. The proposed timing was described by outgoing Department of Higher Education Commissioner Noe Ortega during the Board of Higher Education's Sept. 29 meeting, according to WBUR and the State House News Service (https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/30/massachusetts-private-colleges-higher-ed-closing-risk-schools).

The change would not mean that every school posting a notice is certain to shut down. Under the state's Financial Assessment and Risk Monitoring, or FARM, system, an institution is considered at risk of imminent closure when the commissioner determines that it may be unable to continue operations or substantially meet its obligations to enrolled and admitted students through the current and following academic year. The Massachusetts Department of Higher Education says the system is intended to identify risks, monitor mitigation plans and reduce disruption to students, families, faculty, staff and host communities (https://www.mass.edu/strategic/farm.asp).

The state already requires colleges to alert the Board of Higher Education about known financial liabilities or risks that could lead to an imminent closure or prevent the institution from fulfilling its obligations. The department's FARM materials say those immediate notifications are confidential, while public notice is part of a later process if the institution's financial condition remains sufficiently uncertain after review and risk-mitigation planning. The department also requires private institutions to post annual financial reports and plain-language summaries on their websites.

The proposed Dec. 31 date is meant to make the public-warning process more predictable. WBUR reported that current regulations use Dec. 1 as the annual threshold measurement date for deciding whether a college can meet its obligations for the rest of the current academic year and the next one, while the board currently has flexibility about when after that date to make a determination. Board Chairman Chris Gabrieli said a December determination would reduce the risk that students and staff learn about a potential closure only after they have made plans for the spring semester.

The discussion follows two Massachusetts closures announced near the end of the last academic year. Anna Maria College in Paxton and Hampshire College in Amherst cited financial difficulties in announcing plans to close, WBUR reported. Hampshire's public notice from the Department of Higher Education says the college planned to end academic programming at the end of 2026 while continuing academic programs, residential support and transition services for enrolled students through Dec. 31 (https://www.mass.edu/strategic/documents/2026-04-14-Hampshire-Noitce-Posting-for-DHE-website.pdf). The notice also says the department could not confirm that Hampshire had enough resources to sustain current operations and fulfill obligations through the current and subsequent academic years; that is a regulatory finding, not a claim that every Massachusetts college faces the same condition.

Massachusetts has been building this oversight system since the sudden 2018 closure of Mount Ida College. The department says 24 colleges and universities closed, merged or began winding down between 2014 and 2022, and that the 2019 FARM law and later regulations were designed to improve financial monitoring and closure planning. Those rules can require a contingency plan covering student deposits and records, and in some cases a bond or letter of credit to help protect those obligations. The department's current process describes screening from November through April, review of risk-mitigation plans from June through October, and determinations and contingency planning in November and December.

Officials also said the board plans to add staff and use outside firms to strengthen financial assessments, while revising required training for private-college trustees. The goal, Gabrieli said, is to give students time to identify transfer options, give faculty and staff a reasonable period to seek other work, and reduce the shock to communities that depend on a campus. The timing matters this fall because Ortega's term as commissioner ended Sept. 30 and José Luis Santos began serving as interim commissioner on Oct. 1, according to the department (https://www.mass.edu/).

The public-warning deadline remains a planned policy change rather than a newly announced closure list. The next questions are whether the Board of Higher Education formally adopts the Dec. 31 timetable, which institutions are identified through the annual FARM review, and what mitigation or teach-out plans follow. Until those steps occur, students should not read the proposed deadline as evidence that a particular college is about to close; it is an attempt to move information earlier when the state does determine that a school's finances may threaten its ability to serve students.
author: NorthEast News Desk
